advances: Ordinary continuous equality with a simplex radial body at one interior anchor. The positive chart may have a pole on the boundary of its profile domain.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
**Radial construction.** Drop the boundary values of the positive support. Its boundary is Lebesgue-null and each ray from $0\in U$ meets it in at most one point. The envelope lemma gives positive finite ray integrals, uniform bounds on the sphere and positivity of $g$. Exhaust $U$ by the increasing compact convex neighborhoods $C_j=(1-1/j)(\overline U\cap j\overline{\mathbb B}^r)$ for integers $j\ge2$, where $\overline{\mathbb B}^r$ is the closed unit ball. Each lies in $U$ by scaling toward the interior point $0$. These sets exhaust $U$ since $x/(1-1/j)\in U$ for large $j$ at each $x\in U$. The truncations $f_j=f\mathbf1_{C_j}$ are bounded and upper semicontinuous by interior continuity and closedness of $C_j$, and their extended inverse powers are convex by restriction to $C_j$. Apply 3919a4dbe7ace166 with $p=r$ to each $f_j$. Monotone convergence makes the gauges $[r\int_0^\infty t^{r-1} f_j(tx)dt]^{-1/r}$ decrease to the gauge of $B$, with value zero at the origin. Their pointwise limit is finite and convex, hence continuous. The uniform radial bounds make its unit sublevel a compact convex body with $0$ in its interior. Polar integration identifies its volume and preserves all through-origin cap masses.

**Facet equality.** For $x\in\partial B$, the continuous positive density $r t^{r-1}f(tx)$ on the interior of its ray support has integral one. Its quantile $R_x(v)$, $0<v<1$, is $C^1$ and satisfies $R_x'=g(R_x x)^{r+1}/(rR_x^{r-1})$. For $x_1,x_2$ on a facet and $z=\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2$ with $0<\lambda<1$, write $R_i=R_{x_i}(v)$, $X_i=g(R_i x_i)$ and
$$
T=(\lambda/R_1+(1-\lambda)/R_2)^{-1},\qquad
a_1=\lambda T/R_1,\qquad a_2=(1-\lambda)T/R_2.
$$
Then $\sum_i a_i=1$, $\sum_i a_iR_i=T$, and $Tz=\sum_i a_iR_i x_i\in U$. Differentiation gives $rT'=T\sum_i a_iX_i^{r+1}/R_i^r$. By convexity and weighted Hölder with conjugate exponents $r+1$ and $(r+1)/r$,
$$
rT^{r-1}f(Tz)T'\ge
T^r\frac{\sum_i a_i X_i^{r+1}/R_i^r}{(\sum_i a_i X_i)^{r+1}}
\ge 1.
$$
In the Hölder step factor $a_iX_i=(a_iX_i^{r+1}/R_i^r)^{1/(r+1)}(a_iR_i)^{r/(r+1)}$. The increasing map $T$ starts at zero and stays on the positive ray at $z$. Changing variables shows the integral of the left side over $0<v<1$ is at most one. Thus equality holds at every $v$ by continuity. Integrating up to $v$ gives $R_z(v)=T(v)$. Hölder equality gives $X_1/R_1=X_2/R_2$, so $(1/R_1-1/R_2)'=0$ by the quantile derivative.

**Identification of the chart.** The normalized directional derivative $L$ is finite and sublinear by local convexity of $g$. On a fixed boundary ray, write $f_0=f(0)$ and $t_0=(v/f_0)^{1/r}$. Expansion of $g(tx)$ at zero gives $f(tx)=f_0[1-(r+1)tL(x)+o(t)]$, so the ray CDF is $f_0 t^r[1-r tL(x)+o(t)]$. Taking its $r$th root and inverting yields $R_x(v)=t_0+L(x)t_0^2+o(t_0^2)$ and $1/R_x(v)=1/t_0-L(x)+o(1)$. It follows that $1/R_x(v)+L(x)$ is constant on each facet and that $L$ is affine on each facet, the latter by $1/R_z=\lambda/R_1+(1-\lambda)/R_2$. Every two facets of an $r$-simplex for $r\ge2$ meet, so the reciprocal-quantile function plus $L$ is common to the entire boundary. Set $c=\sum_i\alpha_i L(v_i)\ge L(0)=0$. The unique affine interpolation of the values $L(v_i)-c$ vanishes at zero and is therefore a linear functional $\ell$. Affinity on facets and homogeneity on rays give $L=\ell+c p_B$, and consequently
$$
1/R_x(v)=q(v)-\ell(x)\qquad(x\in\partial B)
$$
for one common function $q$. This proves the claimed uniqueness. Testing at a maximizer of $\ell$ gives $q(v)>\max_B\ell\ge0$. The function $q$ is $C^1$ and strictly decreasing since the quantiles are, respectively, $C^1$ and strictly increasing with positive derivatives. It tends to infinity at $v\downarrow0$. Therefore $\rho(v)=1/q(v)$ increases from zero to $R\in(0,\infty]$, with the claimed bound on $\ell$. At $t=R_x(v)$ the denominator $1+t\ell(x)=tq(v)>0$, and $\Psi(tx)=\rho(v)x$. Since every nonzero point in $U$ occurs before its ray endpoint, this identifies the entire domain and gives the inverse map $\Phi$.

**Profile and converse.** The derivative of $\Phi$ is $(1-\ell(b))^{-1}I+(1-\ell(b))^{-2}b\otimes\ell$, so its determinant is $(1-\ell(b))^{-r-1}$. The transformed inverse power is $\tilde g(b)=(1-\ell(b))g(\Phi(b))$. This is convex: if $b=\sum_i\theta_i b_i$, then $\Phi(b)$ is the combination of $\Phi(b_i)$ with weights $\theta_i(1-\ell(b_i))/(1-\ell(b))$. On a facet ray,
$$
\tilde g(\rho(v)x)=\rho(v)g(R_x(v)x)/R_x(v).
$$
Facet Hölder equality and the shared rays show this is independent of $x\in\partial B$. Thus $\tilde g=h\circ p_B$, with $h$ positive and continuous, convex by restriction to a ray, and nondecreasing since every point of $sB$ for $0\le s<t<R$ is a convex combination of points of $\partial(tB)$, where $\tilde g=h(t)$. Set $F=h^{-r-1}$. On each boundary ray, the substitution $t=\rho/(1-\rho\ell(x))$ gives
$$
t^{r-1}f(tx)\,dt=\rho^{r-1}F(\rho)\,d\rho.
$$
The original ray mass gives normalization and the Jacobian gives the pushforward formula.

Conversely, for finite $R$ the image domain is the convex set $p_B(x)-R\ell(x)<R$, which implies $1+\ell(x)>0$. For infinite $R$, $\ell=0$ and the domain is all of $\mathbb R^r$. The convex, nondecreasing $h$ makes $h\circ p_B$ convex on the open profile domain. Its positive perspective $(1+\ell(x))h(p_B(x)/(1+\ell(x)))$ is convex by the same convex-combination identity with the opposite sign. Extension by $+\infty$ off the domain is convex. The Jacobian and the ray substitution apply throughout the open domains. The ray normalization gives the stated radial body, and polar integration gives finite mass $|B|$, even at an endpoint pole.

**Pole calibration.** For $B=\operatorname{conv}\{(1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1)\}$, $p_B(x,y)=\max(x+y,x-2y,-2x+y)$. Take $R=1$, $\ell(x,y)=x$, $F(t)=4/(1+t)^3$. Then $2\int_0^1 tF(t)\,dt=1$, $\max_B\ell=1$, and the image is $-1/2<y<1$, $x>(y-1)/3$. The density there is $4/(1+x+p_B(x,y))^3$, of mass $|B|=3/2$. At a boundary direction $w$ with $a=\ell(w)$ its CDF before the endpoint is $4[t/(1+(1+a)t)]^2$. The endpoint is $1/(1-a)$ for $a<1$ and infinity for $a=1$. In both cases the limiting CDF is one, and the reciprocal quantile is $2/\sqrt v-1-a$.
statement:
Let $r\ge2$ and let $f$ be a nonnegative Lebesgue density on $\mathbb R^r$ of mass in $(0,\infty)$ with full-dimensional positive support. Assume the extended function $g=f^{-1/(r+1)}$ is convex, taking value $+\infty$ where $f=0$. Translate an arbitrary interior anchor to $0$ and write $U=\operatorname{int}\{f>0\}$. The radial body $B$ has radii
$$
\rho_B(u)^r=r\int_0^\infty t^{r-1}f(tu)\,dt,\qquad u\in\mathbb S^{r-1}.
$$
Then $B$ is a compact convex body containing $0$ in its interior, with volume equal to the mass of $f$, and it preserves every through-anchor closed halfspace mass. If $B$ is a simplex, let $p_B$ denote its Minkowski gauge. In that case there are a linear functional $\ell$, $R\in(0,\infty]$ and a positive continuous $F$ on $[0,R)$ such that $h=F^{-1/(r+1)}$ is convex and nondecreasing and
$$
r\int_0^R t^{r-1}F(t)\,dt=1.
$$
If $R<\infty$, then $R\max_B\ell\le1$. If $R=\infty$, then $\ell=0$. The map $\Phi(b)=b/(1-\ell(b))$ is a bijection from $\{p_B<R\}$ onto $U$, with inverse $\Psi(x)=x/(1+\ell(x))$ and positive denominators on their domains. On $U$,
$$
f(x)=(1+\ell(x))^{-r-1}F\!\left(\frac{p_B(x)}{1+\ell(x)}\right).
$$
Equivalently, $f(x)\,dx$ is the pushforward of $F(p_B(b))\,db$ restricted to $\{p_B<R\}$. Boundary values are immaterial. The functional $\ell$ is uniquely determined: for $L(x)=g'(0;x)/g(0)$, where the derivative is one-sided, $L=\ell+c p_B$ with $c\ge0$. If $v_i$ are the vertices and $0=\sum_i\alpha_i v_i$ is the strictly positive barycentric row of $0$, then $c=\sum_i\alpha_i L(v_i)$.

Conversely, every compact convex body $B$ containing $0$ in its interior and every triple $(\ell,R,F)$ meeting the displayed conditions gives by this construction an integrable density of mass $|B|$ with convex extended inverse $(r+1)$st root and radial body $B$. The finite endpoint equality $R\max_B\ell=1$ is allowed.
title: Critical inverse-power simplex equality is projective radiality
